claim: The hydrothermal vent tubeworm Riftia pachyptila hosts a single 16S rRNA phylotype of intracellular sulfur-oxidizing symbionts.
source: The hydrothermal vent tubeworm Riftia pachyptila hosts a single 16S rRNA phylotype of intracellular sulfur-oxidizing symbionts, which vary considerably in cell morphology and exhibit a remarkable degree of physiological diversity and redundancy, even in the same host.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references the established phylotype of the symbionts.

claim: Riftia pachyptila symbionts vary considerably in cell morphology.
source: The hydrothermal vent tubeworm Riftia pachyptila hosts a single 16S rRNA phylotype of intracellular sulfur-oxidizing symbionts, which vary considerably in cell morphology and exhibit a remarkable degree of physiological diversity and redundancy, even in the same host.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract about symbiont morphological variation.

claim: Riftia pachyptila symbionts exhibit a remarkable degree of physiological diversity and redundancy, even in the same host.
source: The hydrothermal vent tubeworm Riftia pachyptila hosts a single 16S rRNA phylotype of intracellular sulfur-oxidizing symbionts, which vary considerably in cell morphology and exhibit a remarkable degree of physiological diversity and redundancy, even in the same host.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract about physiological diversity.

claim: Small Riftia symbionts actively divide.
source: Metaproteomic analysis, microscopy, and flow cytometry strongly suggest that Riftia symbiont cells of different sizes represent metabolically dissimilar stages of a physiological differentiation process: While small symbionts actively divide and may establish cellular symbiont-host interaction, large symbionts apparently do not divide, but still replicate DNA, leading to DNA endoreduplication.
evidence: This claim is supported by metaproteomic analysis, microscopy, and flow cytometry data presented in the study.

claim: Small Riftia symbionts may establish cellular symbiont-host interaction.
source: Metaproteomic analysis, microscopy, and flow cytometry strongly suggest that Riftia symbiont cells of different sizes represent metabolically dissimilar stages of a physiological differentiation process: While small symbionts actively divide and may establish cellular symbiont-host interaction, large symbionts apparently do not divide, but still replicate DNA, leading to DNA endoreduplication.
evidence: This is inferred from the metaproteomic and microscopy data showing higher abundance of interaction-related proteins in small symbionts.

claim: Large Riftia symbionts apparently do not divide.
source: Metaproteomic analysis, microscopy, and flow cytometry strongly suggest that Riftia symbiont cells of different sizes represent metabolically dissimilar stages of a physiological differentiation process: While small symbionts actively divide and may establish cellular symbiont-host interaction, large symbionts apparently do not divide, but still replicate DNA, leading to DNA endoreduplication.
evidence: This is supported by the absence of dividing large cells in TEM images and lower FtsZ protein abundance in large symbionts.

claim: Large Riftia symbionts still replicate DNA, leading to DNA endoreduplication.
source: Metaproteomic analysis, microscopy, and flow cytometry strongly suggest that Riftia symbiont cells of different sizes represent metabolically dissimilar stages of a physiological differentiation process: While small symbionts actively divide and may establish cellular symbiont-host interaction, large symbionts apparently do not divide, but still replicate DNA, leading to DNA endoreduplication.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing up to 10-fold higher DNA content in large symbionts and detection of DNA replication proteins.

claim: In large Riftia symbionts, carbon fixation and biomass production seem to be metabolic priorities.
source: Moreover, in large symbionts, carbon fixation and biomass production seem to be metabolic priorities.
evidence: This is supported by higher abundance of carbon fixation enzymes (RubisCO, ATP-citrate lyase) and biosynthetic proteins in large symbionts.

claim: Division of labor between smaller and larger symbionts benefits the productivity of the symbiosis as a whole.
source: We propose that this division of labor between smaller and larger symbionts benefits the productivity of the symbiosis as a whole.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation based on the observed metabolic differences between symbiont subpopulations.

claim: Candidatus Endoriftia persephone is a chemoautotrophic gammaproteobacterium.
source: The chemoautotrophic gammaproteobacterium Candidatus Endoriftia persephone, sulfur-oxidizing endosymbiont of the deep-sea tubeworm Riftia pachyptila (here Riftia), provides all nutrition for its gutless host (Cavanaugh et al., 1981; Felbeck, 1981; Hand, 1987; Robidart et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: Candidatus Endoriftia persephone provides all nutrition for its gutless host Riftia pachyptila.
source: The chemoautotrophic gammaproteobacterium Candidatus Endoriftia persephone, sulfur-oxidizing endosymbiont of the deep-sea tubeworm Riftia pachyptila (here Riftia), provides all nutrition for its gutless host (Cavanaugh et al., 1981; Felbeck, 1981; Hand, 1987; Robidart et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: Ca. E. persephone densely populates Riftia's trophosome.
source: Ca. E. persephone (here Endoriftia) densely populates Riftia's trophosome, a specialized organ in the worm's trunk, where the bacteria are housed intracellularly in host bacteriocytes (Hand, 1987).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a previous study.

claim: The trophosome is a specialized organ in the worm's trunk.

claim: In the trophosome, bacteria are housed intracellularly in host bacteriocytes.

claim: Endoriftia symbionts are fueled by the oxidation of reduced sulfur compounds, mainly sulfide.
source: Here, fueled by the oxidation of reduced sulfur compounds (mainly sulfide), the symbionts fix CO2 and produce considerable amounts of biomass, which constitutes the host's source of nutrition (Cavanaugh et al., 1981; Felbeck et al., 1981; Childress et al., 1991; Goffredi et al., 1997a; Girguis and Childress, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: Endoriftia symbionts fix CO2 and produce considerable amounts of biomass.

claim: Host proteins involved in substrate transport from the hydrothermal vent environment to the symbionts include ATPases and carbonic anhydrases for CO2 uptake and conversion.

claim: Riftia has specialized extracellular hemoglobins which simultaneously and reversibly bind sulfide and oxygen.

claim: Symbiont cells in the highly vascularized trophosome contain globules of elemental sulfur.

claim: Trophosome sulfur content is positively correlated with sulfide concentrations in the surrounding water.
source: As trophosome sulfur content is positively correlated with sulfide concentrations in the surrounding water and decreases in the absence of external sulfide (Childress et al., 1991; Robidart et al., 2011; Scott et al., 2012), sulfur in the symbionts likely serves as an energy reserve for times of sulfide deprivation.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: Trophosome sulfur content decreases in the absence of external sulfide.

claim: Riftia symbionts expressed enzymes for both glycogen generation and glycogen degradation.

claim: Individual Endoriftia cells exhibit pronounced morphological diversity, ranging from small rods to small and large cocci.
source: These presumptive subpopulations are likely congruent with symbionts of different cell sizes: Individual Endoriftia cells exhibit pronounced morphological diversity, ranging from small rods to small and large cocci in ultimate proximity to each other within the same host specimen (Hand, 1987; Bright et al., 2000; Bright and Sorgo, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: In individual trophosome lobules, the smallest, rod-shaped symbiont cells are located close to the central blood vessel.
source: In individual trophosome lobules, which measure approximately 200–500 µm in diameter, the smallest, rod-shaped symbiont cells are located close to the central blood vessel, whereas toward the lobule periphery, symbionts gradually increase in size and become coccoid, before they are degraded in the outermost lobule zone.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous microscopy studies.

claim: Four size ranges of symbiont cells were defined: very small (≥2.0 –<3.9 µm diameter), small (≥3.9 –<5.3 µm), medium (≥5.3 –<6.8 µm), and large (≥6.8–20.0 µm).

claim: DNA content in large Riftia symbionts is up to 10-fold higher compared to small symbionts.

claim: Population 1 consists of smaller symbionts.

claim: Population 2 consists of larger symbionts.
source: This suggests that populations 1 and 2 consist of smaller and larger symbionts, respectively.

claim: A total of 1946 symbiont proteins were identified across all sample types.

claim: Sample fractionation by gradient centrifugation facilitated detection of around 60% of the symbiont's theoretical proteome.
source: Our sample fractionation by gradient centrifugation thus facilitated detection of around 60% of the symbiont's theoretical proteome, which encompasses 3182 proteins in PRJNA60889, and yielded substantially higher symbiont protein identification rates than non-enriched trophosome homogenate samples alone (1223 total symbiont protein identifications).
evidence: This is based on comparison of protein identifications with the theoretical proteome.

claim: A total of 465 proteins showed significant differences in relative abundance.

evidence: This is based on statistical analysis using clustering and random forests.

claim: Of all proteins with significant abundance changes, 56% (261 proteins) followed a clear, continuous abundance trend from fraction XS to L or vice versa.

source: Peptidoglycan-recognition proteins, for example, are involved in innate immunity (Kang et al., 1998) and have previously been shown or suggested to participate in symbiotic interactions (Troll et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2009; Royet et al., 2011; Wippler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: Peptidoglycan-recognition proteins have been shown or suggested to participate in symbiotic interactions.
source: Peptidoglycan-recognition proteins, for example, are involved in innate immunity (Kang et al., 1998) and have previously been shown or suggested to participate in symbiotic interactions (Troll et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2009; Royet et al., 2011; Wippler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: Hyou1 has a protective function during hypoxia in human cells.
source: In support of this idea, Hyou1 was shown to have a protective function during hypoxia in human cells (Ozawa et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a previous study.

claim: Beta carbonic anhydrase 1 interconverts bicarbonate and CO2.
source: Moreover, enrichment of beta carbonic anhydrase 1, which interconverts bicarbonate and CO2 (Goffredi et al., 1999; De Cian et al., 2003), suggests that this host protein serves to optimally provide the symbionts with CO2 for fixation.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: TMP214-B was shown to be involved in apoptosis caused by endoplasmic reticulum stress.
source: This would be in line with our previous suggestion that apoptosis-related proteins may play a role in symbiont and bacteriocyte cell death (Hinzke et al., 2019) and is further supported by the fact that TMP214-B was shown to be involved in apoptosis caused by endoplasmic reticulum stress (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a previous study.

claim: Highest individual abundances of various carbon fixation and biosynthesis-related enzymes were found in fraction L.
source: Highest individual abundances of various carbon fixation and biosynthesis-related enzymes as well as highest overall abundances of all biosynthetic categories (including carbon-, amino acid-, lipid-, nitrogen-, and cofactor metabolism; Supplementary file 5) in fraction L suggest that large Endoriftia cells are relatively more engaged in the production of organic material than smaller symbiont cells.
evidence: This is based on metaproteomic data.

claim: Highest overall abundances of all biosynthetic categories were found in fraction L.
source: Highest individual abundances of various carbon fixation and biosynthesis-related enzymes as well as highest overall abundances of all biosynthetic categories (including carbon-, amino acid-, lipid-, nitrogen-, and cofactor metabolism; Supplementary file 5) in fraction L suggest that large Endoriftia cells are relatively more engaged in the production of organic material than smaller symbiont cells.
evidence: This is based on metaproteomic data.

claim: Large Endoriftia cells are relatively more engaged in the production of organic material than smaller symbiont cells.
source: Highest individual abundances of various carbon fixation and biosynthesis-related enzymes as well as highest overall abundances of all biosynthetic categories (including carbon-, amino acid-, lipid-, nitrogen-, and cofactor metabolism; Supplementary file 5) in fraction L suggest that large Endoriftia cells are relatively more engaged in the production of organic material than smaller symbiont cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the metaproteomic data showing higher abundance of biosynthetic enzymes in large symbionts.

claim: RubisCO mRNA signal intensity was notably higher in large symbiont cells than in smaller Riftia symbionts in HCR-FISH analysis.
source: In support of this idea, we (1) observed notably higher RubisCO mRNA signal intensity in large symbiont cells than in smaller Riftia symbionts in our HCR-FISH analysis (Appendix section D, Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This is based on HCR-FISH data.

claim: Higher abundances of glycogen-producing enzymes in fraction L suggest that large symbionts invest relatively more of their biosynthetic capacities in storage of fixed carbon in the form of glycogen than smaller symbionts.
source: Moreover, (3) higher abundances of glycogen-producing enzymes in fraction L suggest that large symbionts invest relatively more of their biosynthetic capacities in storage of fixed carbon in the form of glycogen than smaller symbionts.
evidence: This is inferred from the metaproteomic data showing higher abundance of glycogen synthesis enzymes in large symbionts.

claim: Bright et al., 2000 observed highest 14C carbon incorporation in the Riftia trophosome lobule periphery and lowest short-term incorporation in the lobule center.
source: These observations concur with an autoradiographic study of Bright et al., 2000, who observed highest 14C carbon incorporation in the Riftia trophosome lobule periphery and lowest short-term incorporation in the lobule center
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a previous study.

claim: Sorgo et al., 2002 noted a glycogen gradient in the symbiont cells, with increasing glycogen density from the lobule center toward the periphery.
source: and with results of Sorgo et al., 2002, who noted a glycogen gradient in the symbiont cells, with increasing glycogen density from the lobule center toward the periphery, that is, toward larger symbiont cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a previous study.

claim: Blood flows from lobule periphery to lobule center in Riftia trophosome.
source: A possible explanation for all these findings would be a substrate gradient caused by the direction of the blood flow from lobule periphery to lobule center (Felbeck and Turner, 1995; Figure 6, Appendix section G), which may cause carbon concentrations to be higher around the largest symbionts.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a previous study and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Smaller symbionts produce relatively more sulfur globules for sulfur storage than larger symbiont cells.
source: Smaller symbionts produce relatively more sulfur globules for sulfur storage than larger symbiont cells, as indicated by relatively higher abundance of sulfur globule proteins in fraction XS (Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This is based on metaproteomic data.

claim: Endoriftia's sulfur globules contain elemental sulfur that is formed during sulfide oxidation.
source: Enclosed in a proteinaceous envelope, Endoriftia's sulfur globules contain elemental sulfur that is formed during sulfide oxidation (Wilmot and Vetter, 1990; Pflugfelder et al., 2005; Markert et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: Hand, 1987 noted more sulfur deposits in central (small) than in peripheral (large) Riftia symbionts.
source: Higher numbers of these globules in small symbionts are in agreement with observations of Hand, 1987, who noted more sulfur deposits in central (small) than in peripheral (large) Riftia symbionts.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a previous study.

claim: Activation of stored sulfur involves trafficking proteins such as TusA, which is involved in sulfur transfer to DsrEFH and DsrC.
source: As shown for the free-living thiotrophic model bacterium Allochromatium vinosum, activation of stored sulfur involves trafficking proteins such as TusA, which is involved in sulfur transfer to DsrEFH and DsrC (Stockdreher et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a previous study.

claim: TusA, several DsrC copies, and DsrEFH were all detected with highest abundances in fraction XS.
source: In our study, the highly abundant TusA, several DsrC copies as well as DsrEFH were all detected with highest abundances in fraction XS, thus supporting the idea of relatively more re-mobilization of sulfur and subsequent utilization of reduced sulfur compounds in small Endoriftia.
evidence: This is based on metaproteomic data.

claim: Adenylylsulfate reductase AprAB, ATP-sulfurylase SopT, and sulfide dehydrogenase subunit FccB were detected with higher abundances in fractions XS or S than in M or L.
source: As the highly abundant adenylylsulfate reductase AprAB, the ATP-sulfurylase SopT, and sulfide dehydrogenase subunit FccB were also detected with higher abundances in fractions XS or S than in M or L, one might conclude that sulfide oxidation itself also plays a more prominent role in smaller symbionts than in larger symbionts.
evidence: This is based on metaproteomic data.

claim: SoxZ had highest abundance in fraction L.
source: Larger symbionts may rely relatively more on thiosulfate oxidation – in addition to sulfide oxidation – than smaller Endoriftia, as suggested by highest abundance of SoxZ and detection of several other (low-abundant) Sox proteins in fraction L.
evidence: This is based on metaproteomic data.

claim: Several other (low-abundant) Sox proteins were detected in fraction L.
source: Larger symbionts may rely relatively more on thiosulfate oxidation – in addition to sulfide oxidation – than smaller Endoriftia, as suggested by highest abundance of SoxZ and detection of several other (low-abundant) Sox proteins in fraction L.
evidence: This is based on metaproteomic data.

claim: Endoriftia prefers sulfide but was also shown to oxidize thiosulfate.
source: Although Endoriftia prefers sulfide (Wilmot and Vetter, 1990), it was also shown to oxidize thiosulfate, and may supplement sulfide oxidation with thiosulfate oxidation for energy production (Robidart et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: Expression of the thiosulfate-oxidizing Sox complex was shown to be upregulated in the presence of thiosulfate in A. vinosum.
source: Since expression of the thiosulfate-oxidizing Sox (sulfur oxidation) complex was shown to be upregulated in the presence of thiosulfate in A. vinosum (Grimm et al., 2011), we speculate that higher Sox abundance in large symbionts indicates higher thiosulfate concentrations in the trophosome lobule periphery than in the lobule center.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a previous study.

claim: The Riftia host appears to be able to oxidize toxic sulfide to the less toxic thiosulfate in its mitochondria.
source: The Riftia host appears to be able to oxidize toxic sulfide to the less toxic thiosulfate in its mitochondria (Hinzke et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a suggestion from a previous study.

claim: Rhodanese-like proteins can cleave thiosulfate into sulfite and sulfide and were proposed to be involved in thiosulfate oxidation.
source: The idea of more thiosulfate oxidation in large Endoriftia is further substantiated by highest abundance of six rhodanese family proteins in fraction L, as rhodanese-like proteins can cleave thiosulfate into sulfite and sulfide and were proposed to be involved in thiosulfate oxidation (Hensen et al., 2006; Welte et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: The combined use of both sulfide and thiosulfate has been reported for chemoautotrophic symbionts of snails and mussels.
source: The combined use of both sulfide and thiosulfate has also been reported for chemoautotrophic symbionts of snails and mussels (Beinart et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a previous study.

claim: In symbioses of snails and mussels, thiosulfate oxidation supported carbon fixation just as effectively as sulfide (or even more effectively).
source: In these symbioses, thiosulfate oxidation supported carbon fixation just as effectively as sulfide (or even more effectively).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited study.

claim: Overall abundance of all proteins involved in the symbiont's energy-generating sulfur metabolism remained relatively unchanged across the four fractions.
source: Interestingly, overall abundance of all proteins involved in the symbiont's energy-generating sulfur metabolism, the most abundant of all metabolic categories, remained relatively unchanged across the four fractions (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on metaproteomic data.

claim: Abundances of the Isp-type respiratory H2-uptake [NiFe] hydrogenase large subunit HyaB, a Fe-S oxidoreductase (GlpC), and the hydrogenase expression/formation protein HypE increased from fraction XS to L.
source: In large symbionts, the use of hydrogen may furthermore play a more prominent role than in smaller symbiont cells, as suggested by increasing abundances of the Isp-type respiratory H2-uptake [NiFe] hydrogenase large subunit HyaB, a Fe-S oxidoreductase (GlpC) encoded next to HyaB, and the hydrogenase expression/formation protein HypE from fraction XS to L.
evidence: This is based on metaproteomic data.

claim: Use of hydrogen as an energy source has been described or suggested for free-living sulfur oxidizing bacteria like A. vinosum.
source: Use of hydrogen as an energy source has been described or suggested for free-living sulfur oxidizing bacteria like A. vinosum (Weissgerber et al., 2011), and for a variety of thiotrophic symbionts of marine invertebrates, including Riftia (Petersen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: Above-seafloor hydrogen concentrations in diffuse-flow fluids at the sampling site were reported to be very low (<2 µM).
source: However, above-seafloor hydrogen concentrations in diffuse-flow fluids at our particular sampling site were reported to be very low (<2 µM; McNichol et al., 2018), and it is presently unclear whether and how ambient hydrogen would reach the intracellular symbionts in the trophosome.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a previous study.

claim: H2 was recently suggested to be involved in maintaining intracellular redox homeostasis rather than working as electron donor in the Riftia symbiosis.
source: However, H2 was recently suggested to be involved in maintaining intracellular redox homeostasis rather than working as electron donor in the Riftia symbiosis (Mitchell et al., 2019)
evidence: This is a suggestion from a recent study.

claim: Small Riftia symbionts rely relatively more on the NarGHI-mediated first step of anaerobic respiratory nitrate reduction to nitrite.
source: Our results suggest that small Riftia symbionts rely relatively more on the NarGHI-mediated first step of anaerobic respiratory nitrate reduction to nitrite.
evidence: This is inferred from the metaproteomic data showing higher NarGHI abundance in small symbionts.

claim: Nap-mediated nitrate reduction and all subsequent denitrification steps via NO and N2O to N2 seem to be more prominent in larger symbionts.
source: In contrast, Nap-mediated nitrate reduction and all subsequent denitrification steps via NO and N2O to N2 seem to be more prominent in larger symbionts.
evidence: This is inferred from the metaproteomic data showing higher abundance of Nap and other denitrification proteins in large symbionts.

claim: Endoriftia has the genomic potential for complete denitrification to N2 and was experimentally shown to use nitrate for respiration.
source: While Endoriftia has the genomic potential for complete denitrification to N2 and was experimentally shown to use nitrate for respiration (Hentschel and Felbeck, 1993), our results thus point to differential use of separate parts of this pathway in small and large symbionts.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a previous study.

claim: Expression of membrane-bound nitrate reductase Nar is inhibited by oxygen.
source: Since expression of membrane-bound nitrate reductase Nar is inhibited by oxygen (Moreno-Vivián et al., 1999), highest NarGHI abundance in fraction XS suggests that O2 levels might be particularly low around smaller symbionts.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a previous study.

claim: The periplasmic Nap nitrate reductase is not affected by elevated oxygen concentrations.
source: As the inhibitory effect of oxygen on denitrification was proposed to be largely due to inhibition of nitrate transport across the cytoplasmic membrane to Nar (Denis et al., 1990; Moir and Wood, 2001), the periplasmic Nap nitrate reductase is not affected by elevated oxygen concentrations (Moreno-Vivián et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: Some denitrifying bacteria couple Nap to nitrite reductase Nir, nitric oxide reductase Nor and nitrous oxide reductase Nos under oxic or microaerophilic conditions for aerobic denitrification.
source: Some denitrifying bacteria therefore couple Nap to nitrite reductase Nir, nitric oxide reductase Nor and nitrous oxide reductase Nos under oxic or microaerophilic conditions for aerobic denitrification (Ji et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a previous study.

claim: Nar is an energy-conserving enzyme and generates a proton motive force.
source: Moreover, while Nar is an energy-conserving enzyme and generates a proton motive force, which is potentially advantageous during cell division in small symbionts (see Appendix section B), the periplasmic Nap conserves less energy and does not contribute to the proton gradient (Bell et al., 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a previous study.

claim: The periplasmic Nap conserves less energy and does not contribute to the proton gradient.
source: Moreover, while Nar is an energy-conserving enzyme and generates a proton motive force, which is potentially advantageous during cell division in small symbionts (see Appendix section B), the periplasmic Nap conserves less energy and does not contribute to the proton gradient (Bell et al., 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from a previous study.

claim: Relative abundance of the RNA polymerase sigma factor RpoD decreased from fraction XS to L in S-rich and in S-depleted samples.
source: Relative abundance of the RNA polymerase sigma factor RpoD decreased from fraction XS to L (Figure 3, Supplementary file 3h) in S-rich and in S-depleted samples, pointing to relatively more growth-related activities in small Endoriftia (see also Appendix section B).
evidence: This is based on metaproteomic data.

claim: RpoD is the primary sigma factor for vegetative growth (σ70), which regulates transcription of most genes involved in exponential growth in many bacteria.
source: RpoD is the primary sigma factor for vegetative growth (σ70), which regulates transcription of most genes involved in exponential growth in many bacteria (Helmann and Chamberlin, 1988; Fujita et al., 1994; Ishihama, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: RpoS was not detected in any of the samples.
source: Interestingly, RpoS, the master transcriptional regulator of stationary phase gene expression and antagonist of RpoD, was not detected in any of our samples (although it is encoded in the symbiont genome).
evidence: This is based on metaproteomic data.

claim: RpoS abundance increases upon stress and limitation during transition to the stationary phase in free-living model bacteria.
source: RpoS abundance increases upon stress and limitation during transition to the stationary phase in free-living model bacteria (Hengge-Aronis, 1993; Fujita et al., 1994; Ishihama, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: Calvin cycle and rTCA cycle are in all likelihood expressed in the very same (large) symbiont cells.
source: Calvin cycle and rTCA cycle are in fact in all likelihood expressed in the very same (large) symbiont cells, as suggested by our HCR-FISH experiments (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This is based on HCR-FISH data.

claim: For Rhizobium, a steep O2 concentration gradient inside legume nodules was proposed to be involved in signaling for symbiont differential gene expression.
source: For Rhizobium, a steep O2 concentration gradient inside legume nodules was proposed to be involved in signaling for symbiont differential gene expression (Soupène et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a proposal from a previous study.

claim: Histone-derived antimicrobial peptides were recently proposed to play a role in symbiont cell cycle regulation.
source: Symbiont differentiation in Riftia might furthermore be induced by specific host effectors, for example, histone-derived antimicrobial peptides, which were recently proposed to play a role in symbiont cell cycle regulation (Hinzke et al., 2019), or other compounds that allow Riftia to modulate the symbiont's expression of certain metabolic pathways.
evidence: This is a proposal from a previous study.

claim: Riftia samples for enrichment of symbiont subpopulations were collected at the East Pacific Rise hydrothermal vent field at 9°50' N, 104°17' W in a water depth of about 2500 m during a research cruise with R/V Atlantis in November 2014 (AT26-23).
source: Riftia samples for enrichment of symbiont subpopulations were collected at the East Pacific Rise hydrothermal vent field at 9°50' N, 104°17' W in a water depth of about 2500 m during a research cruise with R/V Atlantis in November 2014 (AT26-23).
evidence: This is a description of the sampling location and time.

claim: Samples for electron microscopy were obtained during a second cruise (AT37-12) at the same site during March-April 2017.
source: Samples for electron microscopy were obtained during a second cruise (AT37-12) at the same site during March-April 2017 (Hinzke et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the sampling for electron microscopy.

claim: Trophosome sulfur content of the specimens was estimated based on the trophosome tissue's color.
source: Trophosome sulfur content of the specimens was estimated based on the trophosome tissue's color: sulfur-rich (S-rich) specimens have a light green or yellowish trophosome, due to the sulfur stored in the symbionts, whereas trophosomes of sulfur-depleted (S-depleted) specimens appear dark green to black (Pflugfelder et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a description of the method used to estimate sulfur content.

claim: Seven healthy-looking Riftia specimens were used for proteomic analyses, of which four had S-rich trophosomes and three had S-depleted trophosomes.
source: For proteomic analyses, we used seven healthy-looking Riftia specimens, of which four had S-rich trophosomes and three had S-depleted trophosomes.
evidence: This is a description of the samples used.

claim: Trophosome sulfur content is positively correlated with habitat sulfide concentrations.
source: Since trophosome sulfur content is positively correlated with habitat sulfide concentrations (Childress et al., 1991; Robidart et al., 2011; Scott et al., 2012), it can serve as an indicator for the energetic situation of the symbiosis at the time of sampling.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.
